answer.summary: Singleton recommends deeply understanding users and involving the right early customers in product development, then repeatedly inspecting the experience from a specific user’s perspective and sweating important details.

sections.heading: Co-create with the right early users
sections.content: Find early users whose needs are pushing the problem forward, learn their challenges and hopes, and bring them into a shared product-development loop. For Stripe Billing, the team worked with existing users including Figma and Slack through shared Slack channels and regular product demonstrations and feedback. They waited until the original alpha group was very happy before considering a broader audience. Singleton also says product builders—especially on developer-focused products—should get to know users well and bring user insight and strategy into the work.

sections.heading: Inspect the product from a specific user’s perspective
sections.content: Use “friction logging”: clearly identify the user whose experience you are modeling, then go through the product in that person’s shoes and record points of friction. Reviews can be done asynchronously, with someone reserving time to inspect the product and make meticulous notes. They can also be conducted together with the product team and cross-functional partners, such as support, walking through the experience and discussing logged issues.

sections.heading: Sweat details at high-stakes moments
sections.content: Be meticulous where users are most likely to need help. Singleton’s example is Stripe API error messages that link directly to the documentation explaining how to solve the problem. He says to use a user-first perspective to decide where to go above and beyond.

answer.summary: Singleton recommends building with carefully chosen early users, learning their needs directly, and iterating with them before expanding to a broader audience. He also emphasizes user-centered craft: experience the product as a specific user, log and review friction, and bring cross-functional perspectives into product development.

sections.heading: Co-create with early users
sections.content: Find the right early users and involve them directly in development. For Stripe Billing, the team partnered with existing customers such as Figma and Slack, whose subscription businesses were pushing the boundaries of what was possible. The team got to know the people operating those systems and their challenges and aspirations, used shared Slack channels, showed them the product regularly, and gathered feedback. It broadened availability only after the original alpha group was very happy with the product.

sections.heading: Make user understanding everyone's job
sections.content: Get to know users well and bring those insights into the product-development loop. Singleton says this is especially important for developer-focused products, where strong product builders are often technically minded and bring user insight and strategy; at Stripe, engineers exercise many skills often associated with PMs. Product work is also cross-functional: engineering, product, design, partnerships, legal, risk, and compliance can all contribute, with PMs often synthesizing user learning and coordinating that work.

sections.heading: Find and fix friction from the user's perspective
sections.content: Use “friction logging”: choose a clearly defined user, put yourself in that person's shoes, and carefully record where the experience causes difficulty. Singleton gives the example of an engineer integrating Stripe Billing at Atlassian. Teams can do this individually and asynchronously, or walk through the product together with its builders and cross-functional partners, record issues as they arise, then discuss which need addressing. He also illustrates meticulous craft with API error messages that link directly to documentation explaining how to solve the problem.
